question: Follow-up on 2024 European Court of Auditors recommendations concerning the identification, mitigation and redress of human rights risks and violation in EUfunded projects

Last year, the European Court of Auditors published the Special Report 17/20241 where it asked the Commission to enhance the respect for the do-no-harm principle in decision-making on any future development action, by: – Conducting systematic risk assessments in the design and formulation phase and translate the mitigating measures into specific activities or outputs indicators; – Drawing up and circulating refined internal procedures for reporting and following up on human rights violations in the context of EU-funded projects; - Analyse information related to human rights risks whether obtained through third-party monitoring or other means.
In its response2 to the Court, the Commission accepted these recommendations and committed to implement them by the end of 2025. 1.

What is the current status of the implementation of these recommendations, in particular the second one on the need to develop clarified internal procedures and how do these procedures complement existing monitoring tools like result-oriented monitoring evaluations and third-party monitoring?
Will these procedures include clear mitigating measures and suspension clauses when human rights violations in the context of EU-funded projects are found?

How will these cover allegations beyond the implementing partners, to include ‘partner of partners’, in line with Article 29(a) of Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument – Global Europe (NDICI) on excluded activities?

answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.1.2026) In June 2025, the Commission formalised an internal procedure to handle human rights complaints in EU-funded projects. The procedure aims to ensure that the complainant receives an acknowledgment of receipt, that a process of verification is conducted and that suspension or termination clauses in contracts are triggered, where necessary and justified.

In May 2025, the Commission developed a document to guide staff in applying the human rights-based approach to migration and forced displacement. This applies at all stages of the project cycle and will be used as the basis for staff training, on human rights indicators and monitoring. These measures build on several layers of monitoring by partners, the contracting authority and through results-oriented monitoring.

All EU projects must identify risks related to human rights. One of the aims of the new guidance is to further strengthen risk identification, assessment and mitigation. Finally, based on standard clauses in EU contracts1, in case human rights violations occur, funding can be suspended or terminated. Those provisions were strengthened in the update to the Commission’s contractual templates in January 2025.

Implementing partners must respect EU values, including human rights, and this obligation also applies to their grant beneficiaries and contractors. Partners shall notify the EU without delay of any credible allegations of violations of human rights affecting implementation. Contracts also provide that these values are to be respected when assets are transferred to third parties at the end of implementation.
